title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
description: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.The histori
body: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters."The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing have yet to comment.No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025."President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September. Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan. The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

schema.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says

title: SpaceX hopes to catch top of Starship rocket for first time
description: Second catch attempt for SpaceX Starship rocketImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Starship rocket launched successfully on FridayByRebecca M
body: Second catch attempt for SpaceX Starship rocketImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Starship rocket launched successfully on FridayByRebecca Morellescience editor and Alison Francissenior science journalist Updated 21 minutes agoSpaceX will decide later whether to try to catch the top part of its huge Starship rocket as it returns to Earth.The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch, and instead the booster diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.The top part, known as the Ship, is due to return to Earth at about 1515 local time (2115GMT) on Saturday.This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 1647 local time (2147GMT) on Friday.The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned. A "go" was initially given by mission control for a catch attempt at the launch tower, but the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The lower stage of the rocket was diverted to the ocean and burst into flames During a livestream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each manoeuvre safely."The top part of the rocket continued its journey to space where it deployed 26 satellites, which form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet.The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off.SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the "chopsticks".Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space.If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.Image source, SpaceXImage caption, A SpaceX lander could take astronauts down to the surface of the Moon Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society."Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said."One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."After SpaceX became a public company earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will Nasa.The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.But it is not the only company working with Nasa. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touchdown.Both companies will also play a key role in the Artemis III mission, which is currently planned for summer 2027 - another challenging schedule.Four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft will attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers during the voyage.Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.Blue Origin had said its spacecraft would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said the US was in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

schema.headline: SpaceX hopes to catch top of Starship rocket for first time

title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
description: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of
body: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow."In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week."Our proposals were almost laughed at."Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire"."The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken."Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.And what of Putin?At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.You can see why.The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

title: New Orleans cruise ship collision: All passengers rescued in 'miracle on the Mississippi'
description: Figure caption, Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New OrleansByAna FaguySome 130 people on a cruise ship docked in Ne
body: Figure caption, Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New OrleansByAna FaguySome 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt.The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort should go to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help"."We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.Were you in the area at the time of incident? Get in touch.Image source, Getty ImagesThere were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side, Moreno said.Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.US President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue had been an "incredible job".Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.Image source, Getty ImagesShips have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what had occurred.Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he had seen the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision."It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."Holford added that he had seen passengers and crew "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.Built in 2015, the vessel has at least four decks.Get in touchIf you were in the area at the time of the incident, please get in touch.

schema.headline: New Orleans cruise ship collision: All passengers rescued in 'miracle on the Mississippi'

title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
description: Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption.The tech firm said
body: Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption.The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected.The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent.Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge. Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again."We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said."We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services."The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem."Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said."In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

schema.headline: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage

title: Chris Van Hollen to challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate leadership
description: US Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party pr
body: US Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections. Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans had voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomed "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".He added that he was "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms and that he had "the votes to continue as Democratic leader". A vote on the new Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes. The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.He wrote that Americans had called on the party to "unrig an economy rigged against working people" in an X post announcing his plan to run."We should not be preserving our institutions if they are not delivering for the American people," he said at a summit in Colorado hosted by majority Democrats. "And we should be making delivering for the American people the single mission of our government, even when that means shaking things up." He added: "This country does not belong to the people who can afford to buy influence. It belongs to all of us. And it's time we govern like that."In recent years, Van Hollen has taken positions popular with those on the left of his party. In 2024, he supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticised the Biden administration over its role in the war in Gaza.Van Hollen - who has served in the Senate for nearly a decade - acknowledged that he was an "underdog" in an interview with MS NOW, but added that he believed the race was "very much in flux".Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have both publicly come out in support of Van Hollen - while others have also called for new leadership.Sanders said he believed Van Hollen "will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families".El-Sayed said the challenger would bring "bold leadership" and lead with both "courage and experience".Others Democrats have publicly backed Schumer.Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada said: "He has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment."Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said: "You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position."

schema.headline: Chris Van Hollen to challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate leadership

title: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for Nvidia chip sales to Megaspeed
description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips,
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but was not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months"."But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China."President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but the Financial Times separately reported that the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia."The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC, external."The real story here should be: did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, according to US media. Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December."Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Huang.Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.They say Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into the US for inspection.A 25% tariff - a levy paid by US importers to the federal government - was imposed on those chips under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security."Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

schema.headline: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for Nvidia chip sales to Megaspeed

title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
description: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volody
body: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.The Ukrainian president's comments on Saturday come after US envoys visited Moscow and an EU summit in Dublin as part of ongoing efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance to deter future threats, but this previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.Zelensky has also consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory, despite Moscow's demands for it to cede the Donbas."The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.There have, however, been recent signs the two can find common ground: last month, US First Lady Melania Trump was able to broker a temporary ceasefire in the the Kherson region to allow for evacuations and aid deliveries.US officials had previously said that Ukrainian Nato membership was off the table.Zelensky said on Saturday that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

schema.headline: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says

title: Aide to pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM badly hurt in Moscow car bomb
description: A car bomb attack in Moscow has wounded a former adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.Sergei Za
body: A car bomb attack in Moscow has wounded a former adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.Sergei Zavorotny, now a journalist and commentator, was behind the wheel of his black Toyota when the explosion happened and Azarov told Russian TV his condition in hospital was "rather critical".The car bomb went off a day after a Russian colonel was killed in another explosion in St Petersburg, and both blasts are seen as part of a series of attacks on military  and prominent figures linked to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Zavorotny, 72, worked as a press aide to Mykola Azarov in Kyiv until 2014.But when pro-Kremlin Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych was toppled from power, Azarov fled Kyiv for Russia and tried unsuccessfully to set up a government in exile.In a 2020 US Senate report on interference in the 2016 American presidential election, Zavorotny is described at the time as an SVR [Russian foreign intelligence] officer involved in influence operations. Russia's Investigative Committee said on Telegram on Friday: "Serhiy Zavorotny, a former adviser to the former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, was injured while driving a car. He was taken to one of the city hospitals, where he is receiving medical care."It added: "A set of necessary investigative actions is being carried out. A number of examinations will be appointed, including medical and explosives."According to several unconfirmed reports, Zavorotny suffered a number of serious injuries after an explosive device was detonated remotely.Russia said the car bombs are the latest in a series of attacks targeting pro-Kremlin figures.On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of St Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military, again after it was attached to the base of the car and detonated remotely.The man targeted in the attack is yet to be named officially, but reputable sources suggest he was a high-ranking figure in the 6th Guards Air and Air Defence Forces Army.Overnight into Friday, Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.Ukrainian authorities said a hospital had been targeted by Russian bombardment.They added that three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were also killed in attacks across southern Odesa and Zaporizhzhia.Russia said a Ukrainian strike on an industrial facility in the central Samara region killed four people.And in the southern Volgograd region another four died after an industrial zone was hit by drones. A further person died in the Bryansk border region, an area that is often fired upon.Ukraine said these were retaliatory attacks in response to Russia's persistent targeting of its cities.

schema.headline: Aide to pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM badly hurt in Moscow car bomb

title: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
description: Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's pa
body: Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it. In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance.They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet.The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran."We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers."In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty.German authorities say Russia was behind the attack.The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police.And Clara Bünger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monster… summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of".The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and Bünger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era."This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers."However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".

schema.headline: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad

title: What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if your flight is affected
description: In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the p
body: In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness.As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems.But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws. Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly. It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund.In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers. However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights. Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason.This includes:a reasonable amount of food and drink (often through vouchers)a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next daytransport to and from that accommodationIf your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.At this stage, it appears that the implementation of new equipment and technology into a decades-old air traffic control system caused it to become overloaded.Duffy said on Friday: "This is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down."Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the system as "a house that's about to be condemned".  "They were adding this software on a system that relies on very tiny, thin copper wires to connect these regional air traffic control systems," O'Brien told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.He said "as the software presented itself to those tiny little wires, it overwhelmed the bandwidth and shut down the system", resulting in "intermittent and inconsistent signals" between air traffic control centres.Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag and adding: "It's going to continue to fail."Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said a patchwork approach to upgrading the system "doesn't work". But Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, also questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel. "You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said "You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added.

schema.headline: What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if your flight is affected

title: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister
description: Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Vikto
body: Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor Orbán, authorities have said.Miklós Seszták, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into Seszták, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said. The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the Orbán rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many Orbán-era policies since entering office.Allegations of corruption and cronyism have long dogged Orbán, who during the course of his tenure turned Hungary into what the EU characterised as an "electoral autocracy".

schema.headline: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister

title: Africa Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
description: Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secur
body: Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory."We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas. "Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026. The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances."Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them. Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa."I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico. She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

schema.headline: Africa Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite

title: Estonia latest country to ban Russian athletes as backlash intensifies
description: Estonia has become the latest country to say it will not allow Russian or Belarusian athletes to compete on its territory as a result of the ongoing w
body: Estonia has become the latest country to say it will not allow Russian or Belarusian athletes to compete on its territory as a result of the ongoing war in Ukraine.It comes after Norway, Finland and Canada made similar announcements.The moves come amid a mounting backlash over the reinstatement of athletes from Russia and Belarus.In September, the International Ski Federation (FIS) relaxed its rules, saying competitors from the two countries would be granted access to its events "provided that they sign a declaration of neutrality".They had previously faced more stringent background checks on any voluntary link or paid duty with the military.Participation remains limited to individual events, with athletes banned from displaying national symbols such as flags, anthems or uniforms.However, it has now emerged that Estonia's government has written to the FIS, claiming that allowing entry to competitors from Russia and Belarus would undermine the country's support of Ukraine, and present an opportunity for propaganda. It said a ban issued in 2022 will be maintained. In a statement issued to BBC Sport, the FIS said it "is committed to offering full support to athletes, national ski associations and local organisers - with most of which we have a long-standing relationship - in the process of navigating what we know to be a very complex situation."With that said, the Individual Neutral Athlete policy is clear in stating that notwithstanding eligibility, the host country visa and entry policies remain in place and are determined solely by the host country. FIS bears no responsibility for denial of visas or entry to any person granted eligibility under the FIS Individual Neutral Athlete Policy."On Thursday, Scandinavian neighbours Norway and Finland both said they would also block visas for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine.Norway is preparing to host the cross-country skiing World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the figure skating world championships in March. The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.This comes in the wake of last month's decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to overturn a ban of Russia by the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), a move condemned by the British, German, Finnish and Czech federations.Russia have been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022, but the Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) then successfully appealed that decision at Cas. The court said that IIHF arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence", but the Hockey Federation of Ukraine said the ruling caused "special outrage".The Canadian government has since informed its hockey authorities that it will not issue visas for Russians to play in next month's World Junior Championship, including those who currently play for teams in Canada, as long as the war continues. A number of countries had said they would refuse to play against Russia, if they were allowed to take part.Despite the controversy, the return of Russia and Belarus to international sport has been gathering pace this year.In March, several athletes from the two countries were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, stating a ban introduced in 2023 after the invasion of Ukraine was "no longer applicable".However, sports federations can still enforce their own eligibility criteria. While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have all removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.Last month, it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships - the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

schema.headline: Estonia latest country to ban Russian athletes as backlash intensifies

title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews ByRiyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatSpanish star Rosalía has ma
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews ByRiyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatSpanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux. The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc. The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement awardIt was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution"."It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Diljit Dosanjh became the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin GrammysAccepting the prize for record of the year, Milo J seemed surprised to have won ahead of strong competition from Karol G, Jorge Drexler, Carin León as well as Rosalía.The 20-year-old took home four trophies in the end and gave a shout out to Argentine folk music.He described Niño as the song "I'm most proud of out of everything I've created so far"."Long live Argentine folk music," he added.Elsewhere, ARIA VEGA was named best new artist and songwriter of the year went to Sara Schell.Additional reporting by Abu Bakar YasinListen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
